newsitem.title: USA: Boeing hopes to sign deal with McDonnell.
newsitem.headline: Boeing hopes to sign deal with McDonnell.

text.p: Boeing Co., faced with billions of dollars in new orders, said Friday it may hire rival McDonnell Douglas Corp. as a contractor.

"We're looking at an arrangement where they could apply some of their resources to some of the work we have on a contractual basis," said Steve Smith, spokesman for Boeing. "We'd like to reach an agreement sooner rather than later but there's no deadline."

Smith said that Boeing's growing backlog was the driving force behind the talks. So far this year the Seattle-based aircraft giant has announced sales of more than 600 aircraft worth over $45 billion, putting pressure on Boeing to come up with a plan for filling all of the orders.
"It would be an effective way to get some assistance to do the type of work we have coming up without trying to do everything ourselves," Smith said.
"We have work and they have resources and we're looking at ways to put the two together ... we think we will have have an agreement that is a win-win for both of us," he said.

Smith declined to specify what work McDonnell Douglas might do for Boeing but analysts speculated Boeing may want the company to work on designs for derivative 767 aircraft freeing up Boeing designers to work on its 777 models.
"It makes a lot of sense, Boeing is approaching capacity on a lot of its production lines," said Paul Nisbet of JSA Research Inc.
Nisbit said the pact could be the first step toward the two firms working closely together but does not expect Boeing to buy Douglas Aircraft.
Boeing's Smith said the proposed pact should not be seen as the first step to Boeing buying Douglas Aircraft.
"We don't discuss rumours about mergers, divestitures or acquisitions so the fact that we're talking about (this) should indicate that's not what we're looking at," he said.
The potential pact is good news for McDonnell Douglas, which recently lost its bid to build the next generation fighter plane for the Pentagon.

In October the company shelved its plans to develop a long-range aircraft. At that time McDonnell said it would focus on its niche market of 100-150 seat airplanes, effectively ending its attempts to compete head-to-head with Boeing.
McDonnell Douglas was not available to comment on the talks.
McDonnell Douglas stock closed up 37.5 cents at $52.875, while Boeing was down 25 cents at $99.375, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
